https://www.politico.eu/article/hackers-.text: Cyberattackers have made “millions” of attempts to take advantage of a critical hole in a building block of the internet, a key cyber service provider said on Thursday. Cybersecurity agencies worldwide scrambled on Wednesday to respond to a flaw in PHP, a foundational computer programming language used to underpin 70% of the internet. Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, an internet services company that is widely used by websites to block cyberattacks — giving it a high level of visibility over what hackers are doing — said in a post on X that it’s seen “millions” of “attempts to exploit” the flaw. Advertisement Advertisement It saw thousands in the 10 hours before the flaw was publicly announced, meaning information must have leaked, then tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after the announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and now millions, Prince said. Amazon’s cloud division also said the flaw is “now being broadly exploited in the wild.” Numerous European government departments took their websites offline as a precaution. As of Thursday morning, key French websites such as the justice ministry and the data protection authority said they were undergoing maintenance. Matthijs van Amelsfort, the head of the Dutch cybersecurity agency, told POLITICO that his agency has no indication that the flaw is “actively being misused” but said that can change, particularly because AI makes it easier to exploit flaws. The agency took its website offline on Wednesday, but it is now back up.

https://hungarytoday.hu/lake-balaton-lif.text: Lake Balaton Lifeguards Look Back on a Busy 2026 Season Lifeguards at Lake Balaton can look back on a busy season: emergency crews provided assistance in 4,370 cases at beaches around the lake between January and early October 2026. A total of 415 lifeguards were active at 61 beaches around the ‘Hungarian Sea’ this year, the Hungarian Water Rescue Service and Volunteer Fire Brigade Association reported. In addition to providing assistance on shore, rescuers had to save 56 swimmers from emergencies in the water. Rescue boats once again formed a key part of the lake’s safety infrastructure. Over the past few months, they responded to 304 incidents, bringing 97 people safely ashore. In a further 40 cases, the focus was on recovering property. These operations included towing boats that had suffered technical failures and righting capsized sailboats. Medical personnel also supported the rescue effort. Boat crews treated 44 patients on the water and at the beaches, while mobile land units were called out 68 times to provide first aid. The specialist diving unit was also called into action on several occasions. In addition to searches for people involved in accidents and lost objects, the technical team worked with divers to recover three sunken boats from Lake Balaton. To ensure a high level of operational readiness over the long term, the organization invested in training and prevention. This year, 85 trainees successfully completed their lifeguard training. Ten stations were also set up along the lake where children’s life jackets could be borrowed free of charge to help protect the youngest visitors. On its social media page, the organization thanked residents and holidaymakers for their trust. At the same time, officials stressed that their work continues even after the end of the peak season. The rescue boats remain available on Lake Balaton around the clock via the BalatonHelp app and the emergency number +36 30 383 8383. The association’s overarching goal remains unchanged: to make Lake Balaton Europe’s safest lake through continuous presence and professional safety services. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-budge.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham will avoid making “arbitrary” cuts to Britain’s rising social security budget, a top Cabinet minister said Friday, as he defended days of mixed government messaging on welfare. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting accused Labour’s opponents — and the Keir Starmer government he served in as health secretary — of not properly thinking through plans to reduce the welfare bill, leading to a collapse in political support. Streeting told the BBC Today program: “I saw it, frankly, after the last general election, when we went too far too fast with an arbitrary figure to cut welfare and when people saw the detail of what that meant for disabled people in our country, the very same people who were saying we need to cut the welfare bill were saying ‘but not like that’.” Advertisement Advertisement He said: “What I do understand from experience, and I’ve seen this experience borne out under both Conservative and Labour governments, is that when you put in place arbitrary targets to cut welfare without a thought-through plan to do so sustainably and responsibly, the plans fall apart.” Spending on U.K. health and disability-related benefits has increased sharply since the Covid pandemic, with the bill for working-age disability benefits in England and Wales increasing from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026 . Former Health Secretary Alan Milburn is leading a report into how to help the estimated one million young people not in employment or education. It is due to be published in November, and the government is also waiting on minister Stephen Timms to make recommendations on disability benefit reform. A previous bid to reduce welfare under Starmer was scrapped after a revolt among Labour MPs. The row was seen as deeply damaging to Starmer’s authority and a sign that the leadership had lost touch with rank-and-file MPs. Streeting’s comments came after an extended back-and-forth between ministers and journalists Thursday over whether Burnham’s government will lower welfare spending before the next general election. Healey was asked by the BBC Thursday whether cuts to the welfare bill would be made before the next election.”There will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we’ll do that in a Labour way,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement But Treasury officials tried to clarify that Healey had not put a date on reductions, with the chancellor telling Channel 4 News shortly afterwards: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.” Streeting said of welfare Friday: “We all agree we’ve got to bring it down, we’ve just got to do it in the right way.” Tories leapt on the confusion yesterday to say Labour were “confused, unserious, and [had] no plan.” Deputy Conservative Chairman Matt Vickers told GB News Friday morning that Healey had given “no answers” on welfare. He added: “The government’s priorities are completely wrong. We need to get in there, sort the ballooning welfare bill, and protect this country properly.”
